ocar.opportunity: Electron-microscopy connectomes can identify the exact neurons and synapses that implement a classic computation, such as visual motion detection in the fly.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy only estimates connections from arbor overlap, and incomplete knowledge of the relevant cells and synapses has long blocked a mechanistic account of motion detection.
ocar.action: Takemura, in Microscopy (2015), reviews EM connectomic reconstructions of the Drosophila visual system, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports that comprehensive EM reconstruction identified the concrete circuit that computes motion signals, with unequivocal connections and precise synaptic counts that arbor-overlap estimates cannot provide.
ocar.future_work: The abstract frames connectomes as a foundation for relating identified circuits to neuronal function; further functional tests are outside this abstract.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies detect motion with a small, well-studied visual system, but seeing every synapse requires electron microscopy. This review says those wiring maps finally named the cells that compute motion.
summaries.intermediate: Takemura (Microscopy, 2015) reviews EM connectomics in the Drosophila brain, with emphasis on visual motion. According to the catalog abstract, recent reconstructions identified the motion-computation circuit because EM yields synaptic counts rather than the estimated contacts of light microscopy. The piece is a review of how such maps underpin functional mechanism, not a new volume. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Ombuya, Guo, and Liu, a review of insect mating behaviors and neuropeptides, not Takemura on fly visual connectomes. Numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Microscopy paper is required for methods, circuit diagrams, and synaptic counts.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies detect motion with a small, well-studied visual system, but seeing every synapse requires electron microscopy. This review says those wiring maps finally named the cells that compute motion.

ocar.opportunity: If neurons carry molecular identification tags, a binding code among cell-surface proteins could explain how partner cells find each other in a crowded neuropil.
ocar.challenge: Drosophila has large immunoglobulin superfamily families whose pairwise binding rules, expression, and synapse-level roles were not mapped together.
ocar.action: Carrillo, Özkan, Menon, and colleagues, in Cell (2015), define a Dpr–DIP interaction network, solve a complex structure, and test Dpr11 and DIP-γ in the larval neuromuscular junction and pupal optic lobe.
ocar.resolution: Twenty-one Dpr proteins bind nine DIPs, with specificity attributed to shape complementarity rather than charge pairs. Each of six examined genes labels a unique neuronal subset. Dpr11–DIP-γ interactions affect NMJ terminals and transmission; in the visual system dpr11 marks yR7 photoreceptors and DIP-γ marks Dm8 targets, and mutants send yR7 terminals past medulla layer M6, with DIP-γ also required for Dm8 survival or differentiation.
ocar.future_work: The discussion treats Dpr–DIP pairs as determinants of connectivity by analogy to SYG-1/SYG-2 and IgLONs, leaving the remaining family members and other circuits for later genetic tests.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly neurons use matching surface proteins as name tags when they choose synaptic partners. Breaking one matched pair scrambles wiring at a muscle synapse and in the eye.
summaries.intermediate: Carrillo et al. (Cell, 2015) report a 21-by-9 Dpr–DIP IgSF binding network whose interface uses shape complementarity, not salt bridges. Six examined genes have distinct larval VNC and pupal optic-lobe patterns. At the NMJ, Dpr11 and DIP-γ regulate presynaptic terminals, trophic responses, and transmission. In the medulla, yR7 (Rh4) cells express dpr11 and their Dm8 targets express DIP-γ; either mutant lets yR7 axons grow beyond layer M6, and DIP-γ is required for Dm8 survival or differentiation.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF is a PMC author manuscript (Cell 163:1770–1782). Only six of 30 family genes are expression-mapped here. ‘Survival or differentiation’ of Dm8 is not resolved. Binding specificity is inferred from structure and biochemistry; the visual and NMJ phenotypes show necessity of one pair, not a complete wiring code. Dprs lack clear mammalian orthologs; DIPs are closest to IgLONs.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly neurons use matching surface proteins as name tags when they choose synaptic partners. Breaking one matched pair scrambles wiring at a muscle synapse and in the eye.

ocar.opportunity: Circuit mapping from fluorescence volumes still depends on turning image stacks into digital neuron trees that can be shared as SWC files.
ocar.challenge: Automatic tracing is not yet reliable, and existing editors did not fully exploit the SWC model for low-cognitive-load 2D/3D reconstruction.
ocar.action: Feng, Zhao, and Kim, in eNeuro (2015), present neuTube 1.0, open-source reconstruction software built around SWC, with parallel 2D and 3D views, seed-based tracing, path search, and editing, compared with Neuromantic and Neurostudio.
ocar.resolution: They argue the WYSIWYG combination of visualization and editing lets users reconstruct from fluorescence data and repair SWC from other tools. The discussion states neuTube results were generally better than those from Neuromantic in their experiment, while stressing that the framework is not a high-throughput tracer.
ocar.future_work: They position the SWC framework as an architecture that can absorb better image-analysis methods while waiting for generally applicable automatic tracing; source is at github.com/janelia-flyem/NeuTu.

summaries.beginner: Turning microscope pictures of neurons into stick-figure trees is still slow, even with computers. neuTube is free software that lets you trace and edit those trees in 2D and 3D at the same time.
summaries.intermediate: Feng, Zhao, and Kim (eNeuro, January 2015) describe neuTube 1.0, SWC-native software with parallel 2D/3D visualization, seed-based tracing, path searching, and extensive editing, aimed at fluorescence reconstructions and repair of files from other packages. They compare it with Neuromantic and Neurostudio and host documentation at neutracing.com. The discussion explicitly says the design does not solve high-throughput tracing (DIADEM-style automation) and that SWC cannot capture geometry finer than optical resolution.
summaries.advanced: Quantitative timing or error rates versus Neuromantic/Neurostudio are not given as single summary statistics in the extract. The stated limitation is SWC-only output. Catalog year is 2015; first published 2 January 2015. Software URLs in the paper should be checked for current availability.

plain_language_summary: Turning microscope pictures of neurons into stick-figure trees is still slow, even with computers. neuTube is free software that lets you trace and edit those trees in 2D and 3D at the same time.

ocar.opportunity: Serial ultrastructural imaging can in principle reconstruct neuronal wiring in central nervous system volumes large enough to be called a connectome.
ocar.challenge: Conventional serial-section TEM is slow, SEM volume methods trade resolution against speed, and huge image stacks still lack automated segmentation.
ocar.action: Ohno, Katoh, Saitoh, Saitoh, and Ohno, in Microscopy (2015), review SEM-based 3D volume EM and tissue preparation that increases heavy-metal contrast, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract argues that SEM serial methods have distinct resolution and speed trade-offs and should be chosen by target size, required resolution, and need for re-observation, while automation of segmentation remains the main bottleneck.
ocar.future_work: The abstract awaits improved acquisition and analysis to relate whole-connectome structure to consciousness, intelligence, and memory.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can now take 3D pictures of brain tissue instead of one thin slice at a time. This review explains those scanning-EM methods and warns that analyzing the pictures is still the hard part.
summaries.intermediate: Ohno and colleagues (Microscopy, 2015) review volume EM toward connectomics. According to the catalog abstract, the key shift is serial imaging with SEM plus heavy-metal staining for contrast, versus classical serial-section TEM. Methods should be matched to tissue size, resolution, and whether sections must be re-imaged; dealing with huge datasets and automating segmentation and 3D reconstruction remain major obstacles. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Collins, Huffman, and Koene, Cell Reports Methods (2025), ‘Comparative prospects of imaging methods for whole-brain mammalian connectomics,’ not Ohno et al. on SEM volume imaging. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can now take 3D pictures of brain tissue instead of one thin slice at a time. This review explains those scanning-EM methods and warns that analyzing the pictures is still the hard part.

ocar.opportunity: Once EM reconstructions yield neuron skeletons, clustering similar shapes can collapse a connectome into cell-type graphs and flag reconstruction errors.
ocar.challenge: Prior complete maps had only hundreds of neurons, and shape clustering that ignores where arbors sit in a layered neuropil will mix distinct types.
ocar.action: Zhao and Plaza, in an arXiv preprint (2014), introduce location-sensitive clustering of skeletonized Drosophila medulla neurons, including affinity-propagation clustering without a preset cluster count.
ocar.resolution: Seventeen clusters reach both precision and recall of at least 80%; nine clusters, including four tangential groups, do not. Merging tangential clusters yields 70.3% precision and 81.3% recall. They treat this as objective confirmation of morphologically distinguishable medulla types and as quality control for missing or partial cells.
ocar.future_work: They note the method can label cells in ongoing reconstructions and detect types missing from some columns; applying it as reconstructions grow is the implied next use.

summaries.beginner: A fly’s visual brain repeats similar cell shapes in each column. This paper groups reconstructed neurons by shape and location so computers can name cell types and catch incomplete tracings.
summaries.intermediate: Zhao and Plaza (arXiv:1409.1892, 2014) cluster Drosophila medulla skeletons with a location-sensitive algorithm and affinity propagation. Table 2 reports 17 clusters with precision and recall both ≥80% and nine poorer clusters; merged tangential cells score 70.3% precision and 81.3% recall. They argue types were generated without a preset cluster number and that clustering finds partial reconstructions and columns missing types. Catalog tags list C. elegans, but the results are medulla EM skeletons.
summaries.advanced: This is an unreviewed arXiv methods paper on existing medulla reconstructions, not a new EM volume. Per-type precision/recall in Table 2 vary widely (e.g. Tm5b 7.7% precision with 100% recall). ‘High-accuracy’ in the abstract is not a single overall score. Catalog organism/dataset fields pointing at C. elegans do not match the paper’s data.

plain_language_summary: A fly’s visual brain repeats similar cell shapes in each column. This paper groups reconstructed neurons by shape and location so computers can name cell types and catch incomplete tracings.

ocar.opportunity: Graph analysis of brains from worm to fly to human can look for shared modular and hierarchical constraints rather than species-specific trivia.
ocar.challenge: Nodes are often treated as identical, yet neurons differ in transmitter, morphology, and genes, and it is unclear where a hierarchy even has a ‘top’ relevant to consciousness.
ocar.action: Kaiser, in a 14 May 2014 Dynamic Connectome Lab technical report, primers structural, functional, and effective connectivity and evolutionary constraints from C. elegans and Drosophila to humans.
ocar.resolution: He states that neural systems are modular and typically hierarchical across levels and species, that topology shapes synchrony, oscillation, and propagation, and that up to 15% of fibres may be unidirectional. Drosophila’s hierarchical versus merely modular status is left open.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion flags linking hierarchy to processing, and studying node heterogeneity (excitation versus inhibition, morphology, expression) as under-investigated compared with hub-versus-regular links.

summaries.beginner: Brains from worms to people can be drawn as networks of nodes and wires. This primer says those networks are built in modules and layers, and that we still do not know how that layering relates to thought.
summaries.intermediate: Kaiser (technical report no. 4, 14 May 2014) surveys connectome graph concepts: directed synapses and tracts, adjacency matrices, and structural versus functional versus effective connectivity, with a cited figure that up to 15% of fibres are unidirectional. The conclusion holds that modular, typically hierarchical organization is common across species, while whether Drosophila is already hierarchical remains open. Topology is said to influence synchrony, oscillation, and activity spread.
summaries.advanced: This is a primer/technical report, not a new reconstruction or statistical meta-analysis. The 15% unidirectional-fibre figure is cited from prior work, not measured here. The PDF extract is OCR-noisy. Consciousness–hierarchy remarks are posed as open questions. Catalog journal/DOI fields are empty.

plain_language_summary: Brains from worms to people can be drawn as networks of nodes and wires. This primer says those networks are built in modules and layers, and that we still do not know how that layering relates to thought.

ocar.opportunity: When scientific datasets outgrow local workstations, remote data-center computing can let many users query subsets efficiently, as cosmology already showed.
ocar.challenge: Connectomic volumes have the same scale-and-complexity problem that once forced astronomy off the desktop.
ocar.action: Burns, Vogelstein, and Szalay, in Neuron (2014), examine how Sloan Digital Sky Survey computational systems were reused at the Open Connectome Project, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract presents cloud-style access as the preeminent model for data-intensive science and lists lessons and top challenges, arguing that success would shrink the time from idea to discovery as SDSS did in cosmology.
ocar.future_work: The abstract outlines expected challenges rather than reporting a completed production architecture.

summaries.beginner: Astronomy already had to store sky maps in giant computer centers instead of on one lab machine. This Neuron piece says brain-wiring images now face the same problem and can reuse those tools.
summaries.intermediate: Burns, Vogelstein, and Szalay (Neuron, 2014) discuss data-intensive computing for connectomics. According to the catalog abstract, they treat cloud computing and high-performance clusters as the working model once data exceed local stores, and they map lessons from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey onto the Open Connectome Project. Success is framed as reducing time from idea to discovery. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Huang et al., Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2019), a single-cell connectome-derived computational model of the Drosophila brain, not Burns, Vogelstein, and Szalay on SDSS-style infrastructure. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract.

plain_language_summary: Astronomy already had to store sky maps in giant computer centers instead of on one lab machine. This Neuron piece says brain-wiring images now face the same problem and can reuse those tools.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM of entire brains, including Drosophila, is usable for synapse-level reconstruction only if section thickness in z is trustworthy.
ocar.challenge: Cutting ultrathin sections has limited thickness precision, so xz views look biologically implausible and pairwise similarity matrices show compressed stretches.
ocar.action: Hanslovsky, Bogovic, and Saalfeld (IEEE ISBI 2015; arXiv 2015) estimate each section’s relative z-position from signal change across the series, tested on ssTEM and FIB-SEM, and release Fiji/TrakEM2 plugins.
ocar.resolution: On a 1000-section FIB-SEM series, similarity estimation took 62.3 s and inference 49.4 s (150 iterations). On 63-section TEM, those steps took 0.6 s and 0.4 s (100 iterations). After random reordering within ±4, recovered z erred by 0.044 px (1.76 nm) on average and 0.13 px (5.2 nm) at most.
ocar.future_work: They plan within-section thickness variation via coarse-to-fine estimation, note that the method can flag missing sections but cannot by itself distinguish loss from gaps, and intend to test whether z-correction helps manual and automated segmentation.

summaries.beginner: When you slice a brain for electron microscopy, the slices are not all the same thickness. This method looks at how much the pictures change from slice to slice and puts each slice back at a more realistic depth.
summaries.intermediate: Hanslovsky, Bogovic, and Saalfeld (ISBI 2015 / arXiv:1411.6970) infer z-coordinates from pairwise section similarity, assuming biological signal changes slowly along z. They demonstrate correction on ssTEM and FIB-SEM, including a 1000-section FIB-SEM run (62.3 s similarity, 49.4 s inference) and 63-section TEM (0.6 s and 0.4 s). A random-order test recovered positions to 0.044 px mean error (1.76 nm). Code is in Fiji and TrakEM2. Catalog year is 2014; the venue year is 2015.
summaries.advanced: Reported nanometer errors are relative to a reference series in their random-order test, not an independent physical thickness gauge. Distinguishing missing sections from true gaps is stated to need further inspection. Within-section thickness is not estimated in this paper. Pairwise similarity can be sampled in parallel; they say sections ≥1000 pixels apart have little influence.

plain_language_summary: When you slice a brain for electron microscopy, the slices are not all the same thickness. This method looks at how much the pictures change from slice to slice and puts each slice back at a more realistic depth.

ocar.opportunity: Automated synapse detection is required if EM volumes are to yield vertices, edges, and attributes of a wiring graph without staining tricks that simplify the images.
ocar.challenge: Synapses are small and low-contrast; prior detectors often assumed isotropic or post-stained tissue that many mammalian EM series do not have.
ocar.action: Gray Roncal and colleagues, in an arXiv paper (v4, 2015) titled VESICLE, present random-forest and CNN synapse detectors that use biological context for anisotropic, non-poststained mammalian EM, plus a large post-stained run on Open Connectome Project infrastructure.
ocar.resolution: They report both approaches beating prior methods on their non-poststained task, with the CNN best overall and the forest more scalable. On a downsampled 5 TB slice of a 20-teravoxel post-stained volume they found about 11.6 million synapses, consistent with published densities of 0.5–1 synapse/µm³, at an estimated operating point of precision 0.69 and recall 0.6 given limited labels. A separate visualization reports 50,000 putative synapses in their volume.
ocar.future_work: They plan region-growing for morphology, supervoxels, CNN architecture and 3D-context tiles, and sampling guided by biological priors.

summaries.beginner: Finding tiny synapses in electron-microscope pictures of mammalian brain is hard, especially when the slices are thick and unstained. VESICLE is computer vision that hunts those contacts using biological context and can run on very large volumes.
summaries.intermediate: Gray Roncal et al. (arXiv:1403.3724v4, 2015) introduce VESICLE for synapse detection in anisotropic, non-poststained mammalian EM, with a random-forest path inspired by human annotators and a CNN path with higher accuracy. On 5 TB of a downsampled 20-teravoxel post-stained dataset they report ~11.6 million synapses and an estimated precision 0.69 / recall 0.6. Code and data are pointed at openconnecto.me/vesicle. The catalog title is an earlier phrasing of the same VESICLE project.
summaries.advanced: Precision/recall on the large post-stained run is an estimate under limited truth; the authors say assessment is ongoing. The 11.6 million and 50,000 synapse counts refer to different processed volumes and should not be conflated. Catalog abstract emphasizes bouton localization; the PDF abstract emphasizes anisotropic non-poststained mammalian data. Kasthuri, Berger, Lichtman, and Fernandez are acknowledged for data and discussion rather than listed as coauthors on the v4 title page.

plain_language_summary: Finding tiny synapses in electron-microscope pictures of mammalian brain is hard, especially when the slices are thick and unstained. VESICLE is computer vision that hunts those contacts using biological context and can run on very large volumes.

ocar.opportunity: Persistent activity that holds a memory can be recorded, but the circuit interactions that link single-cell physiology to behavior are rarely identified by fitting real connectivity.
ocar.challenge: Recurrent circuits have on the order of N² nonlinear synapses, so typical models are built first and only later checked against a few observations.
ocar.action: Fisher, Olasagasti, Tank, Aksay, and Goldman, in Neuron (2013), directly fit synaptic connectivity of an oculomotor short-term memory circuit to anatomical, electrophysiological, and behavioral data together, then run sensitivity analyses.
ocar.resolution: Simultaneous fits indicate complementary roles for synaptic thresholds and neuronal-recruitment thresholds in supplying the nonlinearities needed for the observed circuit behavior, and they argue that anatomical layout can mislead about functional organization.
ocar.future_work: The paper presents the fitting methodology as a way to identify cellular and synaptic memory mechanisms; the extract’s discussion is truncated, so later experimental tests are not recovered here.

summaries.beginner: Some brain circuits keep a memory by staying active after a cue. This team fits a model of an eye-movement memory circuit to many kinds of data at once, instead of building a cartoon and hoping it matches.
summaries.intermediate: Fisher et al. (Neuron, 2013) fit synaptic connectivity in an oculomotor memory circuit jointly to anatomy, physiology, and behavior. Sensitivity analysis is used to argue that synaptic and recruitment thresholds play complementary roles in the nonlinear interactions that generate persistent, memory-related activity. They contrast this with phenomenological models tested on selected observations, and they conclude that anatomy may not mirror functional organization.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract is front matter plus references; the discussion section is not in the supplied text, so quantitative fit errors, neuron counts, and species details beyond ‘oculomotor memory circuit’ are not taken from the extract. Persistent-activity citations in the introduction are background, not this paper’s measurements. Catalog streams tag this as infrastructure; it is a circuit-fitting methods paper.

plain_language_summary: Some brain circuits keep a memory by staying active after a cue. This team fits a model of an eye-movement memory circuit to many kinds of data at once, instead of building a cartoon and hoping it matches.

ocar.opportunity: Serial block-face EM shows cell boundaries and synapses, but segmentation still needs human judgment at a scale automatic methods do not yet own.
ocar.challenge: Expert 3D interfaces do not scale, and crowd tasks must be simple enough for an existing micro-labor pool.
ocar.action: Giuly, Kim, and Ellisman, in Bioinformatics (2013), describe DP2: the Dual Point Decision Process, which asks Amazon Mechanical Turk workers whether two dots lie on the same object, in-plane or across adjacent SBEM slices.
ocar.resolution: Workers answer binary merge questions on cropped superpixels, including a two-frame flicker for across-plane links, at one US cent per decision. Tests include a mouse cerebellar neuropil sample (Dataset 2). Python code is posted for non-commercial use.
ocar.future_work: The application note does not lay out a large production connectome; scaling is implicit in using Mechanical Turk’s existing worker pool.

summaries.beginner: Computers still struggle to outline cells in 3D electron-microscope stacks. This tool pays online workers a penny to say whether two dots sit on the same cell, and many such yes/no answers build the outlines.
summaries.intermediate: Giuly, Kim, and Ellisman (Bioinformatics application note, 2013) distribute SBEM segmentation as Dual Point decisions: workers judge whether two superpixel dots are the same object, either in one plane or in a two-frame animation across slices. Pay is one cent per decision; Dataset 2 is mouse cerebellar neuropil. They contrast this with trained-user 3D tools, scribble tracing, and EyeWire-style volunteer segmentation. Code: sites.google.com/site/imagecrowdseg/.
summaries.advanced: The two-column PDF extract garbles some result numbers (a per-cubic-micron figure for Dataset 2 is split across columns), so accuracy, throughput, and cost totals are not quoted here. This is a short application note, not a full methods trial with extensive statistics. Crowd quality-control details are not in the recovered text.

plain_language_summary: Computers still struggle to outline cells in 3D electron-microscope stacks. This tool pays online workers a penny to say whether two dots sit on the same cell, and many such yes/no answers build the outlines.

ocar.opportunity: Night vision at absolute threshold must pass a single-photon rod signal through rod bipolar (RB) cells and AII amacrine cells without drowning it in noise.
ocar.challenge: How synaptic contacts are allocated so that amplification is local, rather than averaging noise from a wide surround, was not quantified in 3D.
ocar.action: Tsukamoto and Omi, in The Journal of Comparative Neurology (2013), reconstruct serial EM of mouse rod–RB–AII microcircuits and count contacts.
ocar.resolution: In most cases (94%) each rod contacts two adjacent RB cells; each RB is contacted by 25 rods. Each RB axon contacts four or five AII cells via 53 ribbon synapses, so one rod’s signal can appear as 106 replicates at two RB axons. Over 50% of each RB output goes to a preferred AII, with reunion onto few AIIs plus AII–AII gap junctions. The discussion also describes ~100 replicates at RB ribbons and AIS-like AII processes.
ocar.future_work: They interpret the map as a structural basis for high amplification, local adaptation, and regenerative acceleration of AII single-photon responses; those physiological properties are cited, not re-measured here.

summaries.beginner: Seeing in near-darkness means catching a single photon in a rod and getting that whisper to the rest of the retina. This mouse EM study counts how rod, rod-bipolar, and AII cells share synapses so the signal is copied locally instead of smeared.
summaries.intermediate: Tsukamoto and Omi (J. Comp. Neurol. 521:3541–3555, 2013) use serial EM in mouse retina. They report 94% of rods contacting two RB cells, 25 rods per RB, and 53 ribbon synapses from each RB axon onto four or five AIIs (106 replicates at two RB axons). More than half of each RB’s output targets a preferred AII. Dominant connections, reunions, and AII gap junctions are argued to focus signal and limit surround noise. They also document AIS-like AII processes matching prior physiology.
summaries.advanced: Counts are from this reconstruction and should not be generalized to other eccentricities or species without checking the paper’s n and volume. ‘106 replicates’ is their stated product of the dual-RB and ribbon numbers. Functional claims about local adaptation and Na-channel acceleration cite other studies; this paper supplies ultrastructure. Gap-junction coupling is invoked, not newly quantified as conductance.

plain_language_summary: Seeing in near-darkness means catching a single photon in a rod and getting that whisper to the rest of the retina. This mouse EM study counts how rod, rod-bipolar, and AII cells share synapses so the signal is copied locally instead of smeared.

ocar.opportunity: Treating the human brain as a graph of neural elements and interactions gives neuroimaging a large mathematical toolkit.
ocar.challenge: Rapid uptake of graph metrics can undermine explanation if pitfalls in node/edge definition, thresholding, and null models are ignored.
ocar.action: Fornito, Zalesky, and Breakspear, in NeuroImage (2013), review promise, progress, and pitfalls of graph analysis of the human connectome, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract presents graph theory as powerful for anatomical and dynamical characterization while cataloguing unresolved challenges and prevailing workarounds.
ocar.future_work: The abstract places challenges at the forefront of the field rather than closing them.

summaries.beginner: Human brain maps are often turned into networks of regions and links so they can be measured with graph math. This review says that approach is powerful but easy to misuse.
summaries.intermediate: Fornito, Zalesky, and Breakspear (NeuroImage, 2013) review graph analysis of the human connectome. According to the catalog abstract, nodes can be neurons or regions and edges structural, functional, or causal, which brings neuroimaging into graph theory, but pitfalls and unresolved challenges can undermine explanation if not handled carefully. The paper surveys those pitfalls and current solutions. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Spencer et al., a 2026 bioRxiv preprint on the microstructure-weighted human connectome, not Fornito, Zalesky, and Breakspear (2013). Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract.

plain_language_summary: Human brain maps are often turned into networks of regions and links so they can be measured with graph math. This review says that approach is powerful but easy to misuse.

ocar.opportunity: Nanometer EM tracings of neurons and glia are only as useful for physics as the surfaces one builds from them.
ocar.challenge: Visualization meshes from tools such as RECONSTRUCT, TrakEM2, or KNOSSOS are typically not manifold, water-tight, intersection-free, or accurate enough for dynamical simulation.
ocar.action: Edwards, Daniel, Kinney, Bartol, Sejnowski, Johnston, Harris, and Bajaj, in Neuroinformatics (2014 version of a 2013 paper), present VolRoverN, which builds simulation-grade surfaces and skeletons from stacked 2D contours, demonstrated on rat CA1.
ocar.resolution: VolRoverN aims for manifold, water-tight, non-self-intersecting, geometrically accurate meshes extensible to any cell type. Example data are ssEM from postnatal-day-77 male rat hippocampal CA1 at 2 nm in-plane and 45 nm z, 4K × 4K pixels. Surfaces feed MCell, FEM electro-diffusion, and NEURON-style cable models from one mesh source.
ocar.future_work: Quality still depends on input contours; users must repair traces if surfaces reveal errors. Coupled multi-scale MCell/FEM/NEURON simulation is presented as a future use of a shared geometry.

summaries.beginner: Pretty 3D pictures of cells are not the same as shapes a physics simulator can trust. VolRoverN turns traced outlines into sealed, well-behaved surfaces for modeling how ions move in real cell geometry.
summaries.intermediate: Edwards et al. (Neuroinformatics, 2014; DOI 2013) describe VolRoverN for automated surface and skeleton reconstruction from 2D contour stacks, targeting manifold, water-tight, intersection-free meshes. Demonstrations use mature rat CA1 spiny dendrites and axons; the extract specifies P77 perfusion-fixed male rat ssEM at 2 nm × 45 nm, 4K images. Outputs are formatted for MCell, FEM, and cable/NEURON models. Libraries include CGAL, QSlim, OpenGL, and Qt.
summaries.advanced: The PDF is an NIH-PA author manuscript. VolRoverN does not replace tracing; it consumes contours. No quantitative error table versus other meshers appears in the extract. Catalog year is 2013; the manuscript header cites April 2014 pagination. Multi-scale coupled simulation is prospective.

plain_language_summary: Pretty 3D pictures of cells are not the same as shapes a physics simulator can trust. VolRoverN turns traced outlines into sealed, well-behaved surfaces for modeling how ions move in real cell geometry.

ocar.opportunity: Anisotropic EM stacks are often segmented in 2D first; using neighboring sections should fix over- and under-segmentation in hard slices.
ocar.challenge: Textures and topologies vary within and across sections, so independent 2D watershed merge trees make inconsistent choices.
ocar.action: Liu, Seyedhosseini, Ellisman, and Tasdizen (IEEE ICIP / ICCV proceedings 2013) build a watershed merge forest, learn a section classifier for correspondences, update node potentials, and resolve the forest with consistency constraints.
ocar.resolution: On mouse neuropil and ISBI Challenge (Drosophila larva VNC) images, they report testing results improved by over 3.6 percent versus merge-tree results and over 13.1 percent versus thresholding, by borrowing easier adjacent sections.
ocar.future_work: They plan new features for the section classifier and addressing inter-section 3D neuron reconstruction, arguing the reference model also covers many terminations and branchings.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope brain slices are easier to outline if you peek at the slices next door. This method builds a family tree of region merges in each slice and uses neighbors to pick better outlines.
summaries.intermediate: Liu et al. (2013) extend watershed merge trees to a merge forest: each 2D section has a merge hierarchy, a classifier finds likely region correspondences between adjacent sections, and potentials plus consistency constraints yield the stack segmentation. They test mouse neuropil (NCMIR) and Drosophila first-instar VNC (Cardona lab / ISBI). Reported gains are over 3.6% versus merge trees and over 13.1% versus thresholding. Focus is 2D segmentation as a step toward 3D, given ~2–10 nm vs 30–90 nm (SSTEM) anisotropy.
summaries.advanced: The NIH manuscript header lists both ICIP DOI 10.1109/ICIP.2013.6738838 and Proc. IEEE Int. Conf. Comput. Vis. 2013:4069–4073. The ‘percent’ improvements are as stated in the extract without naming the exact metric in that paragraph. This is intra-section segmentation using inter-section cues, not a finished 3D reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope brain slices are easier to outline if you peek at the slices next door. This method builds a family tree of region merges in each slice and uses neighbors to pick better outlines.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans wiring diagram is small enough that graph spectra can be used to ask whether the connectome is fractal, small-world, or otherwise ordered.
ocar.challenge: Self-similarity is easy to claim and hard to distinguish from random, tree, or rewired-fractal controls.
ocar.action: Reese, Brzoska, Yott, and Kelleher, in PLoS ONE (2012), analyze a Laplacian of the 279-neuron giant component, with eigenvalue counting, eigenfunction localization, path length, clustering, and matched synthetic graphs.
ocar.resolution: They confirm small-world characteristics and highly localized eigenfunctions that could suggest self-similar motifs, but conclude the network is not random, tree-like, or fractal, while still highly ordered. They offer Laplacian-construction algorithms as a toolbox.
ocar.future_work: Further work is required to interpret localization; they stress that 279 nodes limit network analysis and that the same tools should be applied when larger complete maps exist.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s 300-cell nervous system is a complete wiring list. Mathematicians here test whether that network looks like a fractal, a random scribble, or a small world, and they find order without true fractal structure.
summaries.intermediate: Reese et al. (PLoS ONE, 2012) take the Varshney et al. C. elegans schematic, build a Laplacian on the 279-neuron giant component of the 302-neuron nervous system, and compare eigenvalue counting, eigen-coordinates, small-world metrics, and eigenfunction localization with random graphs, trees, fractals, and rewired fractals. Conclusions: small-world, localized eigenfunctions, not random/tree/fractal, but highly ordered. Chemical-synapse directionality makes the raw adjacency non-symmetric before Laplacian construction.
summaries.advanced: ‘Giant component of 279’ and ‘302 neurons’ are as stated; later reannotations of the worm connectome are not used. Fractal-like hints are explicitly not a claim that the graph is a fractal. No single clustering-coefficient or path-length number is quoted in the recovered conclusions paragraph. This is graph analysis of an existing map, not new EM.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s 300-cell nervous system is a complete wiring list. Mathematicians here test whether that network looks like a fractal, a random scribble, or a small world, and they find order without true fractal structure.

ocar.opportunity: Because dendritic spines are excitatory synaptic sites, disease-related spine changes are circuit changes in partners, astrocytes, and organelles, not only counts and shapes.
ocar.challenge: Light-level spine metrics miss nanometer relationships that require volume EM.
ocar.action: Kuwajima, Špaček, and Harris, in Neuroscience (2013 version of a 2012 paper), review ssEM studies of pathological neuropil and practical perfusion-fixation for high-quality volumes.
ocar.resolution: They argue ssEM is the best current route to place spine pathology in 3D neuropil context, and they detail adult-rat perfusion (artificial ventilation, up to 180 mmHg, brief oxygenated buffer then mixed aldehydes in cacodylate) versus ≤30 s diaphragm-to-fixative for mice or juvenile rats to limit hypoxia.
ocar.future_work: They caution that animal models capture only some aspects of heterogeneous human disease, so patient ultrastructure should set the context for model findings.

summaries.beginner: Counting how many dendritic spines look stubby or long is not enough to understand brain disease. This review says you need 3D electron microscopy to see each spine with its partner axon and nearby support cells.
summaries.intermediate: Kuwajima, Spacek, and Harris (Neuroscience, 2013; DOI 2012) review serial-section EM of spine pathology in surrounding neuropil, including synapses, astrocytes, and organelles. They treat renewed ssEM methods and computational 3D tools as enabling this literature. A methods-heavy section specifies perfusion-fixation aimed at avoiding hypoxia and osmotic artifact (adult rats under ventilation, pressure up to 180 mmHg; mice/juveniles without ventilation, fixative within 30 s). Phosphate-buffer particulates are noted as a reason to prefer cacodylate in their protocol.
summaries.advanced: This is a review plus protocol commentary, not a new pathology cohort. The supplied PDF is an NIH author manuscript (final pagination Neuroscience 251:75–89, 2013). Catalog year is 2012. Quantitative disease-specific spine counts are not synthesized as a single table in the extract. Clinical-network claims are framed as anatomical substrates, not demonstrated here.

plain_language_summary: Counting how many dendritic spines look stubby or long is not enough to understand brain disease. This review says you need 3D electron microscopy to see each spine with its partner axon and nearby support cells.

ocar.opportunity: Macroscale wiring diagrams of rat and mouse can be assembled from the tract-tracing literature if names in different atlases can be translated.
ocar.challenge: Independent parcellation schemes rarely define interrelationships, and resliceable 3D atlas alignment was still immature, so studies on different maps cannot be merged naively.
ocar.action: Bota, Dong, and Swanson, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2012), present BAMS (Brain Architecture Knowledge Management System) and a rat macroconnectome with more than 50,000 inserted connectivity reports.
ocar.resolution: BAMS stores qualitative comparisons inserted by anatomists or collated from papers, then generates large-scale connection matrices online. The 2012 rat matrix uses a different classification scheme than earlier versions and exceeds the 50,000-report benchmark.
ocar.future_work: They intend spatial attributes (injection and label sites), a re-implemented reliability inference engine, completion of the rat literature connectome, and macroconnectomes for mouse, monkey, and human, plus molecule and cell modules.

summaries.beginner: Rat and mouse brain maps use many different names for the same regions, so connection lists cannot simply be pasted together. BAMS is a public database that translates those names and builds large wiring tables from published tracing studies.
summaries.intermediate: Bota, Dong, and Swanson (Front. Neuroinform., 2012) describe BAMS (brancusi.usc.edu/bkms) as infrastructure for mammalian macroconnectomes. Incompatible atlases are handled by expert or collator annotation rather than mature 3D resampling. The updated rat macroconnectome exceeds 50,000 connectivity reports under a new classification. The workflow is map rigorously, insert and annotate, then generate matrices online. Macroconnections are axonal links between gray-matter regions treated as nodes.
summaries.advanced: Fifty thousand is a count of inserted reports, not unique verified synapses or a complete matrix fill-in. Strengths are qualitative. 3D inter-atlas models are explicitly not ready. URL longevity should be checked. This is literature collation, not new tracing or EM.

plain_language_summary: Rat and mouse brain maps use many different names for the same regions, so connection lists cannot simply be pasted together. BAMS is a public database that translates those names and builds large wiring tables from published tracing studies.

ocar.opportunity: Most tract-tracing exists in rat, so the amygdala’s intrinsic and extrinsic wiring can be compiled into a weighted directed graph for network analysis.
ocar.challenge: Graph statistics depend on how regions sit in an ontology, and original papers often omit injections that would complete the picture.
ocar.action: Schmitt, Eipert, Philipp, Kettlitz, Fuellen, and Wree, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2012), import a rat amygdala meta-connectome into neuroVIISAS and compute local and global metrics.
ocar.resolution: The intrinsic amygdala graph is described as small-world and scale-free. Highest combined in- and out-degree: anterior cortical nucleus (72), posterior nucleus (45), anterior basomedial nucleus (44). The posterior nucleus has minimal Shapley rate and is called most important. Complete reciprocal motifs exceed randomizations. Superficial regions are flagged as densely interlinked for internal regulation.
ocar.future_work: They note that including non-amygdala-focused papers should raise validity, while synaptic-level spatiotemporal dynamics remain outside this tract-tracing meta-graph.

summaries.beginner: The amygdala is a cluster of nuclei that traffic emotion and memory signals. This team gathered published rat tracing studies into one directed network and asked which nuclei sit at the center.
summaries.intermediate: Schmitt et al. (Front. Neural Circuits, 2012) build weighted digraphs of rat amygdala intrinsic and extrinsic connections in neuroVIISAS. They report small-world and scale-free intrinsic topology; degree leaders anterior cortical (72), posterior (45), and anterior basomedial (44) nuclei; and minimal Shapley rate for the posterior nucleus. They reconstruct a fear-conditioning pathway but find more subregion interconnectivity and reciprocity than some optogenetic circuit sketches assumed. The supracapsular BST lateral part has high Shapley importance despite degree 13, so they warn against reading Shapley in isolation.
summaries.advanced: This is a literature meta-study, not new tracing. Edge presence and weights inherit publication bias and ontology choices. ‘Scale-free’ and ‘small-world’ are authors’ network-statistic claims on the compiled graph. Behavioral roles of hub regions are mapped onto other studies, not tested here. Extract discussion notes synaptic dynamics as a limitation of connectome analysis at this scale.

plain_language_summary: The amygdala is a cluster of nuclei that traffic emotion and memory signals. This team gathered published rat tracing studies into one directed network and asked which nuclei sit at the center.

ocar.opportunity: A whisker column in rat cortex is a defined 3D object whose thalamocortical synapses can be counted by cell type and soma location.
ocar.challenge: Somata and dendrites of excitatory types intermingle, so innervation cannot be read from layer labels alone, and structure–function links may differ by type.
ocar.action: Oberlaender, de Kock, Bruno, Ramírez, Meyer, Dercksen, Helmstaedter, and Sakmann, in Cerebral Cortex (2012; advance 2011), reconstruct lemniscal VPM axons and excitatory neurons of a barrel column, objectively classify nine excitatory types, and compare predicted innervation with whisker-touch responses.
ocar.resolution: Thalamocortical connectivity depends strongly on cell type and 3D soma location. Lemniscal afferents can account for some type- and location-specific subthreshold and spiking responses after passive touch in layer 4, but not for other types, for example in layer 5. The result is a quantitative 3D prediction of cell-type-specific VPM wiring.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s conclusions paragraph is truncated; the abstract already implies that additional pathways are needed where VPM innervation does not explain responses.

summaries.beginner: Each whisker on a rat’s snout maps to a cortical column. This study rebuilds the 3D wiring from thalamus onto nine kinds of excitatory cells in one column and asks which cells that thalamic input can actually explain.
summaries.intermediate: Oberlaender et al. (Cereb. Cortex 22:2375–2391, 2012) reconstruct VPM lemniscal axons and excitatory somata/dendrites in an anatomically defined rat vibrissal column, classify nine excitatory cell types, and estimate thalamocortical synapse numbers and distributions. Overlapping dendritic territories still yield type- and location-specific innervation. Correlation with in vivo passive-whisker-touch responses accounts for some layer-4 patterns but not, for example, layer 5. Keywords: barrel cortex, dendrite morphology, in vivo spiking, VPM innervation.
summaries.advanced: Synapse numbers in the abstract are ‘estimated’ from reconstructions registered to a standardized column, not a fully dense EM connectome. Functional comparison is to passive whisker touch, not active whisking. The supplied extract cuts off in Conclusions, so later caveats in that section are not used. Inhibitory cells are outside the nine excitatory types.

plain_language_summary: Each whisker on a rat’s snout maps to a cortical column. This study rebuilds the 3D wiring from thalamus onto nine kinds of excitatory cells in one column and asks which cells that thalamic input can actually explain.

ocar.opportunity: If the largest cortical interneuron class, PV+ cells, follows a simple local connectivity rule onto pyramids, inhibition can be modeled as a dense blanket rather than a fine-scale specific graph.
ocar.challenge: Inhibitory circuit diagrams were still poorly mapped; apparent specificity might be an artifact of sparse sampling.
ocar.action: Packer and Yuste, in Journal of Neuroscience (2011), use two-photon RuBi-Glutamate uncaging to map PV+ interneuron connections onto pyramidal cells across mouse cortical areas and layers.
ocar.resolution: They find locally dense PV+→PC connectivity; in many experiments every nearby PV+ cell connected to every local PC sampled. PV+ cells contacted PC pairs similarly whether or not the pyramids were synaptically connected to each other. They conclude the architecture is an unspecific, densely homogeneous matrix over nearby pyramids, and probably for neocortical inhibition in general.
ocar.future_work: Generalization from PV+ to all inhibition is stated as a conclusion, not a multi-class mapping; other interneuron types remain to be compared with the same method.

summaries.beginner: A major class of inhibitory cells in mouse cortex appears to connect to essentially all nearby excitatory cells, not to a hand-picked few. The authors suggest local inhibition is more like a dense mesh than a precise wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: Packer and Yuste (J. Neurosci. 31:13260–13271, 2011) optically map parvalbumin-positive interneurons onto pyramidal cells with two-photon RuBi-Glutamate uncaging. Connectivity is locally dense across areas and layers; many experiments show complete local PV+→PC sampling. There is no evidence that PV+ cells prefer synaptically coupled PC pairs. The authors propose an unspecific dense matrix as a canonical inhibitory microcircuit. Related prior work from the lab on somatostatin cells in frontal cortex is cited as similarly dense.
summaries.advanced: The extract jumps from introduction to references, so quantitative connection probabilities, distances, and n are not recovered from a Discussion. ‘Probably neocortical inhibition in general’ is an extrapolation from PV+ (and cited SST) maps. Uncaging demonstrates functional connections, not synapse ultrastructure. ‘Unspecific’ means no detected fine-scale PC-pair bias, not that biology is random at all scales.

plain_language_summary: A major class of inhibitory cells in mouse cortex appears to connect to essentially all nearby excitatory cells, not to a hand-picked few. The authors suggest local inhibition is more like a dense mesh than a precise wiring diagram.

ocar.opportunity: A complete wiring diagram requires tracing neuronal processes through enormous optical or EM image sets.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation and tracing remain a major bottleneck; new optical methods add image-analysis problems of their own.
ocar.action: Lu, in Neuroinformatics (2011), reviews automated tracing algorithms for fluorescence and electron microscopy connectomics, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract surveys recent progress in automated tracing and discusses challenges posed by novel optical imaging.
ocar.future_work: Open tracing challenges under new optical techniques are flagged rather than solved.

summaries.beginner: To map every wire in a circuit you must follow each branch through a mountain of microscope images. This review covers computer programs that try to do that tracing in light and electron microscopy.
summaries.intermediate: Lu (Neuroinformatics, 2011) reviews automated neuronal tracing for connectomic reconstruction from fluorescence and EM, according to the catalog abstract, and discusses image-analysis challenges from newer optical methods. It is a review of algorithms, not a new tracer. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Li, Hu, Wang, Sun, and Quan, Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2025), a neuronal imaging dataset for deep-learning reconstruction of single-neuron axons, not Lu (2011) on tracing algorithms. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract.

plain_language_summary: To map every wire in a circuit you must follow each branch through a mountain of microscope images. This review covers computer programs that try to do that tracing in light and electron microscopy.

ocar.opportunity: A complete connectivity matrix might be recovered statistically from sparsely localized fluorescent synaptic markers instead of tracing every process in EM.
ocar.challenge: Dense EM reconstructions of even C. elegans-scale circuits were still extremely slow; larger animals looked worse.
ocar.action: Mishchenko, in Journal of Neuroscience Methods (2011), proposes randomized genetic targeting of synaptic markers plus compressive sensing to reconstruct the connectivity matrix, tested in simulations on the C. elegans EM diagram, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract claims the worm wiring diagram could in principle be re-obtained in 1–7 days of imaging and analysis versus at least 1–2 years for alternative approaches then, and discusses possible Drosophila applications.
ocar.future_work: Application to larger organisms is discussed as prospective in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Instead of photographing every synapse with electron microscopy, this paper proposes randomly tagging synapses with fluorescent markers and reconstructing the wiring with compressive sensing. Simulations on the worm map suggest a much faster path, if the method works in real tissue.
summaries.intermediate: Mishchenko (J. Neurosci. Methods, 2011) describes sampling physical connectivity with anatomical fluorescent synaptic markers placed by randomized genetic targeting, then recovering a high-resolution matrix with compressive sensing. According to the catalog abstract, simulations using the existing C. elegans EM diagram suggest 1–7 days versus 1–2 years for alternative reconstructions of that diagram, with possible extension to Drosophila. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Barnes, Bonnéry, and Cardona, PLOS ONE, on synaptic counts approximating synaptic contact area in Drosophila, not Mishchenko’s compressive-sensing reconstruction proposal. Timing claims (1–7 days vs 1–2 years) are from the catalog abstract’s simulations, not a wet-lab reconstruction. Independent reading of the Methods paper is required.

plain_language_summary: Instead of photographing every synapse with electron microscopy, this paper proposes randomly tagging synapses with fluorescent markers and reconstructing the wiring with compressive sensing. Simulations on the worm map suggest a much faster path, if the method works in real tissue.

ocar.opportunity: The developing mammalian neuromuscular junction is a complete, optically accessible connectome in which synapse elimination and axon layout can be quantified.
ocar.challenge: Automatically tracking individual axons through complex 3D microscopy of the innervation field was unsolved.
ocar.action: Srinivasan, Li, Zhou, Lu, Lichtman, and Wong, in Bioinformatics (ISMB 2010), present AxonTracker-3D, an interactive 3D tracking and labeling tool for reconstructing axonal structures across the innervation field.
ocar.resolution: They argue the tool yields quantitative morphology—trajectories, branching, geometry, spatial relations of axon groups—with a balance of ease of use and accuracy. Availability is given as cbi-tmhs.org/AxonTracker/.
ocar.future_work: They intend data mining on branch number versus segment length, whether axon spatial distributions are random, and optimal motor-neuron layout using extracted wiring diagrams.

summaries.beginner: At the junction between nerve and muscle, you can see whole wiring diagrams in the light microscope, but following each axon by hand is painful. AxonTracker-3D is software to trace those axons in 3D with a person in the loop.
summaries.intermediate: Srinivasan et al. (Bioinformatics 26:i64–i70, ISMB 2010) introduce AxonTracker-3D for interactive tracking and labeling of axons in neuromuscular-junction connectomes, aimed at synapse-elimination and organizational questions in mammalian CNS development. They emphasize organizational specificity of axons and the need for individual labels. Planned analyses include branch–length relationships and spatial statistics of motor axons. The paper is a software/methods report in the ISMB proceedings issue.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s discussion is split across columns; quantitative accuracy metrics and dataset sizes are not recovered as summary statistics. The download URL is from 2010 and may be stale. This reconstructs light-microscopy NMJ axons, not CNS EM synapses. Catalog tags it as graph analysis; the deliverable is a tracker.

plain_language_summary: At the junction between nerve and muscle, you can see whole wiring diagrams in the light microscope, but following each axon by hand is painful. AxonTracker-3D is software to trace those axons in 3D with a person in the loop.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans uniquely pairs a complete wiring diagram with emerging neuron-specific gene-expression profiles, so molecular logic of connectivity can be asked computationally.
ocar.challenge: Connecting those two data types requires identifying synergistic gene sets, not single-gene correlates.
ocar.action: Varadan, Miller, and Anastassiou, in Bioinformatics (ISMB 2006), present EMBP (Entropy Minimization and Boolean Parsimony) and an information-theoretic synergy measure, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports preliminary results on public data in which identified gene sets show exceptionally high synergy, taken as evidence of joint pathway involvement, and presents the strategy as improving as more neuron-specific expression appears.
ocar.future_work: The abstract expects more accurate results as expression atlases grow and hopes for clues to universal interconnectivity mechanisms.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring diagram can be lined up with which genes each neuron turns on. This paper’s math looks for groups of genes that together predict who connects to whom.
summaries.intermediate: Varadan, Miller, and Anastassiou (Bioinformatics / ISMB, 2006) introduce EMBP to find synergistic gene sets whose joint expression predicts C. elegans neural connectivity, plus a multivariate synergy measure. According to the catalog abstract, preliminary public-data results show exceptionally high synergy, interpreted as joint pathway involvement, with accuracy expected to rise as neuron-specific expression improves. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Qiao, ‘Deciphering the genetic code of neuronal type connectivity through bilinear modeling’ (a recommendation-system-style covariance model on transcriptomes), not Varadan, Miller, and Anastassiou (2006) EMBP. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. No gene-set names or synergy values are quoted because they are not in that abstract.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring diagram can be lined up with which genes each neuron turns on. This paper’s math looks for groups of genes that together predict who connects to whom.

ocar.opportunity: The midget–parvocellular pathway is the high-acuity route of primate central retina; its OFF midget bipolar output synapses can be counted across species and color-vision genotypes.
ocar.challenge: Whether dichromatic and trichromatic marmosets, and macaques, use the same midget synaptic numerology was unclear.
ocar.action: Jusuf, Martin, and Grünert, in The Journal of Comparative Neurology (2006), quantify OFF midget bipolar output synapses in marmoset and macaque, as described in the catalog abstract.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports 1:1 midget bipolar to midget ganglion contacts in marmoset, consistent with Old World primates. Output synapses per axon terminal: dichromatic marmoset 10–71 (mean 29.7 ± 12.4 SD, n=104 cells, two animals), trichromatic marmoset 12–86 (28.6 ± 11.7, n=108, one animal), macaque 9–48 (26.5 ± 9.3, n=118, one animal), all unimodal, suggesting comparable midget circuitry.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not add experiments beyond this comparison.

summaries.beginner: In the center of a primate eye, midget cells carry fine detail toward color vision. This study counts synapses from OFF midget bipolar cells in marmosets and macaques and finds similar numbers whether the marmoset has two or three cone types.
summaries.intermediate: Jusuf, Martin, and Grünert (J. Comp. Neurol., 2006) study OFF midget bipolar connectivity in Callithrix jacchus (di- and trichromatic) and Macaca fascicularis. According to the catalog abstract, marmoset midget bipolars contact midget ganglion cells 1:1. Mean output synapses per terminal are about 30 in both marmoset color-vision types and about 27 in macaque, with overlapping ranges and unimodal histograms. Markers: CD15 (marmoset bipolars), recoverin (macaque), ribbon proteins or GluR4, plus retrograde midget ganglion labels from parvocellular LGN in marmosets. Summaries follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Miyagishima, Grünert, and Li, Visual Neuroscience (2014), on S-cone signal processing in the inner plexiform layer, not Jusuf et al. (2006) on midget–parvocellular synapses. Synapse counts and n above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Catalog dataset tags list mouse retina; the paper is primate.

plain_language_summary: In the center of a primate eye, midget cells carry fine detail toward color vision. This study counts synapses from OFF midget bipolar cells in marmosets and macaques and finds similar numbers whether the marmoset has two or three cone types.

ocar.opportunity: A vertebrate morphology atlas with excitatory/inhibitory identity and dendrite–axon polarity would let putative mesoscopic connectomes be built across the whole larval nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Prior vertebrate single-neuron reconstructions were limited in coverage and cell-type labels.
ocar.action: Du, Yue, Chen, and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2025; version posted 24 March 2026), reconstruct a nervous-system-wide larval zebrafish morphology atlas and define morphotypes and putative inter-type and interregional connectomes, served via ZExplorer/iBrAVE.
ocar.resolution: They report more than 20,000 reconstructed neurons from more than 13,400 animals, spanning CNS and PNS, about 24.5% of brain excitatory and inhibitory neurons in a common space, and more than 500 E and I morphotypes. Projection analyses show laterality and directionality biases and modular innervation; network analyses yield motifs, hubs, and sensorimotor pathways. Connectivity is inferred from thresholded dendrite–axon proximity after registration.
ocar.future_work: Limitations include transgene variability, coarse parcellation, and the proximity-not-synapse assumption. They call for EM, transcriptomics, intersectional genetics, and functional tests. Data and code deposits are listed as available upon publication.

summaries.beginner: This team traces more than twenty thousand larval zebrafish neurons, marks them as excitatory or inhibitory, and lines them up in one standard fish brain. From how axons sit next to dendrites they sketch who might talk to whom, with the caveat that nearby is not the same as a synapse.
summaries.intermediate: Du et al. (bioRxiv 10.1101/2025.06.06.658008, version 24 March 2026) present a larval zebrafish single-neuron morphology atlas with E/I identity and polarity: >20,000 reconstructions from >13,400 animals, ~24.5% of brain E/I cells, >500 morphotypes, plus putative inter-cell-type and interregional connectomes. They describe laterality/directionality biases, modular innervation, hubs, and sensorimotor pathways, with visualization in iBrAVE/ZExplorer. Cytoarchitecture uses genetically encoded markers and manual counting.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint (not certified by peer review in the banner). Putative synapses are proximity-based, not EM-verified; the authors state dependence on registration, polarity assignment, and a contact assumption. Coverage is ~24.5% of brain E/I neurons, not a complete census. Catalog year is 2026. Accession numbers for CZRC lines are listed as pending in the extract.

plain_language_summary: This team traces more than twenty thousand larval zebrafish neurons, marks them as excitatory or inhibitory, and lines them up in one standard fish brain. From how axons sit next to dendrites they sketch who might talk to whom, with the caveat that nearby is not the same as a synapse.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical circuits show both heterogeneous degrees (as in the mouse EM connectome) and diverse intrinsic timescales; a mechanistic link would explain multiplexed computation.
ocar.challenge: Standard random recurrent nets treat neurons as exchangeable and do not produce degree-dependent memory.
ocar.action: Zenari, Taffarello, Mazzucato, Maritan, and Suweis (arXiv:2603.04149, 2026) build a configuration-model recurrent net with tunable degree heterogeneity and partial synaptic-weight symmetry, derive heterogeneous dynamical mean-field theory, and instantiate topology from the MICrONS cubic-millimeter mouse connectome.
ocar.resolution: hDMFT yields a degree-scaled non-Markovian self-coupling that broadens activity timescales; degree heterogeneity lowers critical gain and localizes unstable modes on hubs. Under broadband input, slow hubs act as integrators. On MICrONS-matched topology they report a positive Spearman correlation between in-degree and resting-state calcium timescale, ρ ≈ 0.16 (p ≈ 10⁻⁴). In-degree after cutoff kmin = 14 is fit by a truncated lognormal (μ = 3.83, σ = 0.69).
ocar.future_work: The theory identifies hubs in partially symmetric nets as a substrate for multiplexed timescales; extending beyond resting-state calcium and the fitted degree cutoff is implied by the empirical analysis choices.

summaries.beginner: Some neurons in cortex are social hubs with many incoming wires, and some are slow thinkers. This theory says those facts are linked: hub wiring plus partly symmetric synapses naturally creates a mix of fast and slow cells, matching mouse connectome recordings.
summaries.intermediate: Zenari et al. (arXiv 2603.04149, 2026) introduce a configuration-model recurrent network and heterogeneous DMFT in which partial weight symmetry plus degree heterogeneity produce a degree-dependent memory kernel and a wide timescale distribution. Stability analysis says heterogeneity lowers critical gain and concentrates unstable modes on hubs. Instantiating MICrONS topology, they relate in-degree to intrinsic timescale (HWHM of resting calcium autocorrelation), Spearman ρ ≈ 0.16, p ≈ 10⁻⁴. Calcium filtering is acknowledged as a relative, not absolute, timescale measure.
summaries.advanced: Catalog DOI/journal fields are empty; this is an arXiv theory-and-data paper. ρ ≈ 0.16 is statistically significant but modest; it does not imply in-degree is the dominant timescale cause. kmin = 14 is chosen by minimizing KS distance to a truncated lognormal. The supplied extract includes methods for MICrONS analysis more than a narrative discussion. Sensory-driven epochs are excluded by design.

plain_language_summary: Some neurons in cortex are social hubs with many incoming wires, and some are slow thinkers. This theory says those facts are linked: hub wiring plus partly symmetric synapses naturally creates a mix of fast and slow cells, matching mouse connectome recordings.

ocar.opportunity: If the brain can sense sugar already in the oesophagus and immediately relax crop muscles, ingestion can be gated on a fast interoceptive loop rather than only by postingestive metabolism.
ocar.challenge: Neural mechanisms of brain–digestive-tract communication during a sip remain poorly mapped.
ocar.action: Cui, Meiselman, Thornton, and Yapici, on bioRxiv (3 September 2024), identify Gr43a enteric sensory neurons, IN1 brain neurons, and enteric motor neurons as a gut–brain–gut circuit in Drosophila, using physiology plus FlyWire connectome analysis.
ocar.resolution: Enteric Gr43a neurons monitor oesophageal sugar and excite IN1s, promoting high-sugar consumption. Connectome analysis (putative IN1s, n=4 in FlyWire) places IN1s as a core ingestion circuit onto crop-entry motor neurons. Persistent IN1 activation with sugar-rich food coincides with continuous inhibition of those motor neurons, relaxing crop muscles for large-volume intake.
ocar.future_work: The preprint frames the loop as a mechanism for rapid monitoring and motor control across metabolic states; broader circuit tests and published-journal versions are outside this extract. Fewer than 4% of imaged flies were excluded for health or motion artifacts.

summaries.beginner: Flies decide how much sugar to swallow using sensors in the food tube that talk to brain cells, which then relax the crop—the fly’s stretchy storage stomach. It is a gut–brain–gut loop, not only a later metabolic aftertaste.
summaries.intermediate: Cui et al. (bioRxiv 10.1101/2024.09.02.610892, 3 Sept 2024) report that oesophageal enteric neurons expressing the sugar receptor Gr43a excite ingestion-regulating IN1 brain neurons, which in turn output to enteric motor neurons at crop entry. FlyWire/Codex analysis of putative IN1s (n=4) supplies the synaptic skeleton of this loop. IN1s stay active on sugar-rich food while enteric motor neurons are inhibited, relaxing crop muscle. Catalog abstract OCR renders the neuron name as ‘IN18’; the PDF methods consistently use IN1.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. Connectome claims rest on n=4 putative IN1 meshes and automatic synaptic-site detection in FlyWire, not a full EM circuit proof of all enteric partners. ‘IN18’ in the catalog abstract is treated as an extraction artifact for IN1s. Exclusion of <4% of flies is stated; sample sizes otherwise live in figure legends not fully recovered here.

plain_language_summary: Flies decide how much sugar to swallow using sensors in the food tube that talk to brain cells, which then relax the crop—the fly’s stretchy storage stomach. It is a gut–brain–gut loop, not only a later metabolic aftertaste.

ocar.opportunity: Cellular-resolution tracing connectomes of marmoset cortex can be turned into eigenmodes that should constrain how resting fMRI activity is allowed to look.
ocar.challenge: How monosynaptic anatomical connectivity shapes cortical activity, and whether those modes transfer to human homologs, was unclear.
ocar.action: Xia, Liu, Li, Meng, Yang, Chen, and Liao, in Nature Communications (2024), decompose the marmoset neuronal-tracing connectome with graph signal processing and compare CC-eigenmodes to resting-state BOLD.
ocar.resolution: Cellular connectome eigenmodes constrain marmoset rs-fMRI activity and reveal a dorsal-posterior coupled versus ventral-anterior decoupled gradient that recapitulates microstructural and hierarchical organization. The same marmoset-derived modes are reported to help infer spontaneous activity and functional connectivity of homologous human areas, unlike rewired or non-homologous controls in the figures.
ocar.future_work: The discussion begins from quantifying how BOLD is bounded by CC-eigenmodes and relating temporal fluctuations to anatomy; the extract cuts off in figure panels, so later limitations are not fully recovered.

summaries.beginner: A marmoset brain’s tracing-based wiring diagram can be turned into vibration-like patterns (eigenmodes) that predict how resting activity is allowed to spread. Those same patterns also help guess activity in matching parts of the human brain.
summaries.intermediate: Xia et al. (Nat. Commun. 15:2289, 2024) apply graph signal processing to a marmoset neuronal-tracing connectome, yielding CC-eigenmodes that constrain resting BOLD. They describe a spatial gradient from coupled dorsal-posterior to decoupled ventral-anterior cortex, aligned with micro-structure and hierarchy. Cross-species tests use homologous landmarks; figures contrast empirical CC graphs with rewired graphs and non-homologous regions when reconstructing activity and functional connectivity (reconstruction accuracy plotted versus number of eigenmodes; N=5 in figure panels).
summaries.advanced: Do not read axis tick labels (e.g. 0.9, 0.86) as a single reported accuracy score; they are figure-scale markings in a two-column extract. Eigenmodes constrain BOLD; they do not prove monosynaptic causality of each fluctuation. Human inference is about homologous areas, not a claim that the marmoset graph is the human connectome. Tracer-based edges are mesoscale, not EM synapses.

plain_language_summary: A marmoset brain’s tracing-based wiring diagram can be turned into vibration-like patterns (eigenmodes) that predict how resting activity is allowed to spread. Those same patterns also help guess activity in matching parts of the human brain.
